EXCERPT: say that we have a prediction we have a model of how the brain works we look at the brain stage we make a prediction about what the person is experiencing and then ask them what they are experiencing in fact we've done this test where we've had models of brain states where you save can we predict what a person is going to choose option A or option B and they've predicted it with 80 percent success that they can
CRITIQUE: Strongest feature: Jump directly explains how private experience remains scientifically tractable: investigators use neural models to predict reports or choices and subsequently compare those predictions with the subject's independently supplied answer. Principal limitation: successful prediction establishes dependable mapping but may leave open whether experience is identical with, realized by, or merely dependent upon the measured neural state; the cited eighty-percent result concerns choice prediction. Live burden: he must provide discriminating tests between physical realization and interactionist dependence, clarify exactly what outcomes were predicted, and justify the ontological inference from methodological success. Locked score: 83 points, reflecting excellent reply contact, empirical orientation, precision, and substantial comparative force, tempered because reliable prediction alone does not completely settle the metaphysical identity question.

MOVE: pro-nondegreed-personhood
EXCERPT: saying if a person born with 10% of a brain is not 10% of a person and if cutting my arms and leg off legs off don't make me 50% of a person then it follows that personhood is none degreed and then it would also follow from that that personhood must cannot be grounded in just the physical parts of the body that you said that makes a person so a person can't just be something physical
CRITIQUE: Strongest feature: Hernandez contrasts continuously variable bodily composition with apparently categorical personhood, using limb loss and reduced brain volume to raise a genuine question about unity and numerical identity. Principal limitation: categorical classifications can supervene upon graded physical structures or organizational thresholds, and the examples do not establish that every amount of neurologically significant loss leaves personhood wholly unchanged. Live burden: he must define personhood, separate moral status from cognitive capacity, defend strict non-gradability across difficult cases, and establish why only a nonphysical soul can ground the category. Locked score: 67 points, recognizing intuitive relevance and a concrete metaphysical challenge, while reflecting weak warrant for the universal premise and an unsupported inference from physical variability to transcendent personhood.

MOVE: con-personhood-spectrum
EXCERPT: you're born without a brain you're not a person because you don't have a brain you have no consciousness you have no interaction you can't live so you're not a person at what point do you go from like 10 percent of a brain 5 percent where does that line draw I have no idea it's still a spectrum and that whether or not we call it a hard distinction between the person not person isn't
CRITIQUE: Strongest feature: Jump tests Hernandez's categorical premise against neurologically significant limiting cases, noting that consciousness, interaction, viability, and other personhood-relevant capacities plausibly diminish across a physical spectrum. Principal limitation: graded underlying capacities do not automatically establish that personhood itself is graded, because a categorical status may arise at a threshold whose precise boundary remains epistemically uncertain. Live burden: he must specify constitutive criteria, explain how their aggregation produces personhood, and address moral equality and persistence without presupposing that neurological dependence settles the ontology. Locked score: 75 points, crediting substantial reply contact, empirically grounded pressure, and appropriate acknowledgment of boundary uncertainty, while reflecting the unresolved distinction between continuous person-making properties and discrete personal status.

MOVE: pro-transcendent-ground-of-personhood
EXCERPT: person had not a degree property that you cannot ground your personhood or anything physical which means being a person is not necessarily until two are tied to something physical then you would have to grind it in something transcend it beyond the body that's not
CRITIQUE: Strongest feature: Hernandez states the intended metaphysical consequence of his personhood argument clearly, proposing an invariant transcendent ground where changing bodily composition appears insufficient to explain categorical personal status. Principal limitation: the conclusion largely repeats the disputed premise, assumes that graded physical realization cannot support discrete categories, and does not independently demonstrate that the proposed transcendent ground exists or constitutes a soul. Live burden: he must exclude threshold, organizational, biological, psychological, and relational accounts, establish criteria for the transcendent bearer, and explain its connection to identity and value. Locked score: 55 points, reflecting direct relevance and understandable structure, but substantial deficiencies in evidential warrant, alternative elimination, responsiveness to Jump's threshold possibility, and the central inference beyond the body.

MOVE: con-discrete-physical-personhood
EXCERPT: that's all a neurology question I can grant it for the sake of the arguments a personhood is a discrete either yes or no question and say that can still all be explained by the physical you don't need any supernatural for that at all
CRITIQUE: Strongest feature: Jump answers Hernandez on the strongest available formulation by granting discrete personhood arguendo while denying that discreteness requires nonphysical realization, thereby exposing the constructive's invalid transition. Principal limitation: asserting neurological explanation remains schematic because no threshold, organizing mechanism, or persistence criterion is supplied, and the term supernatural does not precisely track every proposed nonphysical soul. Live burden: he must provide principled physical criteria for one unified person, handle gradual replacement and duplication cases, and demonstrate explanatory superiority rather than bare logical compatibility. Locked score: 75 points, reflecting efficient dialectical strategy, direct relevance, and charitable concession, while reserving credit because the positive physical account remains largely promissory and does not resolve the deepest unity questions.

MOVE: pro-conscious-subject-to-soul
EXCERPT: the soul because when I argue for the soul out I argue two points consciousness is not physical and then I argue that consciousness is possessed by something namely a person's like I possess consciousness so what is the I that indexical word then I argue that I am not identical to my brain and body I'm more than a brain and body and then I argue soul so given those arguments
CRITIQUE: Strongest feature: Hernandez finally articulates the cumulative bridge to the motion, identifying the soul with the first-person subject that possesses consciousness and is allegedly irreducible to brain and body. Principal limitation: the move depends upon earlier property and privacy arguments whose irreducibility conclusions remain contested, while possession language does not establish that consciousness requires a separate substantial owner. Live burden: he must demonstrate subject unity beyond physical integration, exclude property-dualist and emergent alternatives, and provide identity conditions showing how this possessor persists and interacts. Locked score: 69 points, recognizing direct relevance, synthetic value, and conceptual clarity, but reflecting limited independent warrant and an inference that substantially redescribes the desired conclusion instead of conclusively establishing nonphysical existence.
